(2018) showed that scalable deep learning models could effectively leverage electronic health records for clinical predictions. These successes, however, have also highlighted the "black box" nature of many high-performing models, raising concerns about transparency and interpretability in critical medical contexts.

To address these concerns, the field of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged, with a particular focus on developing methods that make AI decisions more transparent to end-users. Guidotti et al. (2018) and Tjoa et al. (2019) provide comprehensive surveys of XAI techniques, emphasizing the unique challenges and requirements of medical applications. In particular, local explanation methods—which aim to clarify individual predictions rather than global model behavior—have gained traction for their ability to support clinical decision-making. Lundberg et al. (2017) introduced SHAP, a unified framework for interpreting model predictions, which has been widely adopted for its theoretical grounding and practical utility. Similarly, Guidotti et al. (2019) explored both factual and counterfactual explanations, further enriching the toolkit for local interpretability.

Within the healthcare domain, several studies have tailored XAI methods to specific medical tasks. Panigutti et al. (2019) proposed approaches for explaining multi-label black-box classifiers in health applications, while Papanastasopoulos et al. (2020) developed explainable deep-learning ensembles for classifying estrogen receptor status from breast MRI, demonstrating the value of interpretable models in medical imaging. Farahani et al. (2022) reviewed XAI applications in neuroimaging, highlighting the growing importance of transparency in complex diagnostic workflows. Metta et al. (2021) advanced the field by introducing exemplar- and counterexemplar-based explanations for image classifiers, specifically targeting skin lesion labeling, which aligns closely with the needs identified by Gouda et al. (2022) in their work on deep learning for skin cancer detection.

The LORE (Local Rule-Based Explanations) technique, which is central to our work, builds on the tradition of rule-based and counterfactual explanations. Spaccapietra (2008) discussed the foundational role of data semantics in supporting meaningful explanations, while Brefeld et al. (2020) explored knowledge discovery frameworks that facilitate interpretable machine learning. Jampani et al. (2012) assessed computational visual attention models on medical images, underscoring the importance of aligning model explanations with human perceptual processes.

Despite these advances, the trade-off between interpretability and predictive performance remains a persistent challenge, as noted by Zhang et al. (2018) in their discussion of deep learning definitions and limitations. Our work situates itself at the intersection of these research directions, seeking to advance local explanation methods—particularly LORE—in healthcare settings, where transparency and trust are paramount. By building on the insights and methodologies established in prior work, we aim to contribute to the ongoing effort to make AI-driven healthcare both effective and interpretable.

(2015) demonstrated the potential of interpretable models—such as generalized additive models—in predicting clinical outcomes, laying foundational groundwork for intelligible machine learning in healthcare. However, as deep learning models became more prevalent, their black-box nature raised significant concerns regarding transparency and trust (Guidotti et al., 2018).

To address these concerns, numerous explanation methods have been developed, ranging from global model interpretability to local, instance-based explanations. Saleem et al. (2022) provide a comprehensive survey of global interpretation techniques for deep neural networks, while local explanation methods—offering case-specific insights—have been recognized as particularly critical for clinical adoption. Metta et al. (2022) introduced exemplars and counterexemplars as a means of providing intuitive, image-based explanations for skin lesion classifiers. Building on this, Metta et al. (2023) investigated the impact of such explanations on user trust, showing that transparent deep learning models can enhance clinician confidence in automated diagnosis.

The design of explanations for non-expert users is equally important, as highlighted by Larasati et al. (2023), who demonstrated that meaningful, context-sensitive explanations can positively influence patient trust in AI medical systems. Panigutti et al. (2022) further explored how different explanation types affect advice-taking behavior in clinical decision support scenarios, underscoring the need for explanations tailored to user expertise and preferences.

In the context of medical imaging, deep learning models have shown remarkable promise for tasks such as COVID-19 diagnosis (Yoo et al., 2020; Boutorh et al., 2021) and skin lesion segmentation (Mirikharaji et al., 2022). Boutorh et al. (2021) compared various XAI models for COVID-19 diagnosis using CT-scan images, emphasizing the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability. Meanwhile, Hamm et al. (2023) demonstrated the value of interactive explanation interfaces, enabling radiologists to better understand and trust AI-driven prostate cancer diagnosis at MRI.

Transparent reporting is also essential for trustworthy AI. Mitchell et al. (2018) introduced the concept of Model Cards to standardize the disclosure of model characteristics, limitations, and intended use cases, fostering accountability and reproducibility in healthcare AI. Furthermore, the availability of large, high-quality datasets such as MIMIC-III (Johnson et al., 2016) and MIMIC-IV (Johnson et al., 2023) has been instrumental in advancing research on explainable models by providing realistic, diverse clinical data for benchmarking and validation.

Despite these advances, challenges remain in balancing model complexity, clinical performance, and explainability. Brefeld et al. (2020) highlighted the ongoing need for scalable methods that can extract actionable knowledge from increasingly complex healthcare data. As the field moves towards greater transparency, future work must continue to refine local explanation techniques that are accurate, context-aware, and user-centered, ensuring that AI systems in healthcare are both powerful and trustworthy.

prompt: On the Reconstruction of Face Images from Deep Face Templates
text:
## Related Work

The security and privacy of biometric templates, particularly in face recognition systems, have been longstanding concerns in the research community. Early work by Yuen et al. (2002) explored face representation using independent component analysis, laying the groundwork for understanding how facial features can be encoded in compact forms. Building on the question of template invertibility, Adler (2003) demonstrated that sample images could be independently restored from face recognition templates, highlighting the potential privacy risks associated with template storage. Mignon et al. (2013) further advanced this line of inquiry by reconstructing faces from their signatures using RBF regression, providing concrete evidence that face templates can be vulnerable to inversion attacks.

Beyond direct inversion, researchers have also investigated the susceptibility of face recognition systems to various attack vectors. Galbally et al. (2010) examined the vulnerability of face verification systems to hill-climbing attacks, showing that iterative optimization techniques can be used to approximate templates and compromise system security. Similarly, Feng et al. (2014) introduced masquerade attacks on transform-based binary-template protection schemes, leveraging perceptron learning to bypass template protection mechanisms. These studies collectively underscore the need for robust template protection and motivate the exploration of reconstruction attacks in the context of modern deep learning-based systems.

With the advent of deep neural networks, face recognition has achieved unprecedented accuracy, but new challenges have emerged regarding the security of deep face templates. Sun et al. (2014) demonstrated that deeply learned face representations are sparse, selective, and robust, which has implications for both recognition performance and template security. The development of advanced architectures, such as deep residual networks (He et al., 2015), and the adoption of efficient machine learning libraries like MXNet (Chen et al., 2015), have further accelerated progress in this domain. However, these advances also raise questions about the invertibility of deep templates and the feasibility of reconstructing original face images from them.

In parallel, the broader field of biometric security has seen comprehensive reviews, such as Biggio et al. (2015), which examined biometric system security from the adversarial machine-learning perspective. These works emphasize the importance of understanding both the strengths and vulnerabilities of biometric systems in adversarial settings. Additionally, research on feature extraction and representation, including the use of Histograms of Oriented Gradients (Déniz-Suárez et al., 2011) and Local Quantized Patterns (Hussain et al., 2012), as well as probabilistic modeling approaches like Probabilistic Linear Discriminant Analysis (Shafey et al., 2013), has contributed to the development of more robust recognition systems, though often without directly addressing template invertibility.

Finally, foundational advances in neural network training and architecture, such as the introduction of Rectified Linear Units (Nair et al., 2010), have enabled the training of deeper and more expressive models, which are now standard in face recognition pipelines. While these technical improvements have led to significant gains in recognition accuracy, they also necessitate renewed scrutiny of template security, particularly in light of recent findings on template reconstruction.

In summary, the intersection of face template security, inversion attacks, and deep learning-based recognition systems forms a vibrant area of research. The present work builds on these foundations by proposing a neighborly de-convolutional neural network (NbNet) for reconstructing face images from deep templates, addressing the critical question of template invertibility in state-of-the-art systems.

Face recognition has been a central topic in computer vision for decades, with early approaches focusing on holistic and statistical representations. Notably, Belhumeur et al. (1996) compared Eigenfaces and Fisherfaces, demonstrating the effectiveness of class-specific linear projections for recognition tasks. Similarly, Yuen et al. (2002) explored independent component analysis for face representation, while Déniz-Suárez et al. (2011) leveraged Histograms of Oriented Gradients to capture local facial features. The FERET evaluation methodology introduced by Phillips et al. (1997) provided a standardized benchmark, facilitating the comparison and advancement of face recognition algorithms. As datasets and evaluation protocols matured, works such as Liao et al. (2014) further benchmarked large-scale unconstrained face recognition, highlighting the challenges posed by real-world variability.

With the advent of deep learning, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for face recognition, achieving unprecedented accuracy. Simonyan et al. (2014) introduced very deep convolutional architectures that have since become foundational in the field. Subsequent works, such as Wolf et al. (2011), addressed recognition in unconstrained video settings, while Huang et al. (2012) proposed methods for learning facial alignment from scratch, further improving robustness. Chen et al. (2013) investigated the "blessing of dimensionality" in high-dimensional feature spaces, proposing efficient compression techniques for face verification. Optimization techniques such as Adam (Kingma et al., 2014) have also played a crucial role in training deep models effectively.

As face recognition systems have become more accurate, concerns regarding their security and privacy have grown. Galbally et al. (2010) demonstrated the vulnerability of face verification systems to hill-climbing attacks, revealing that adversaries could iteratively refine inputs to match stored templates. Biggio et al. (2015) provided a comprehensive review of adversarial machine learning in biometric recognition, discussing various attack vectors and countermeasures. Feng et al. (2014) specifically examined masquerade attacks on transform-based binary-template protection, highlighting the risks associated with template inversion. These works collectively underscore the importance of understanding and mitigating vulnerabilities in biometric systems.

Template inversion attacks, which aim to reconstruct original biometric data from stored templates, have received increasing attention. Zeiler et al. (2011) introduced adaptive deconvolutional networks for feature learning, laying the groundwork for subsequent efforts in reconstructing images from deep representations. The challenge of reconstructing face images from deep templates is particularly acute given the high dimensionality and nonlinearity of modern embeddings. Ghosh et al. (2003) discussed the behavior of correlated random vector generation in high dimensions, which is relevant to understanding the complexity of template inversion in deep feature spaces.

Within this context, our work builds upon these foundations by proposing a neighborly de-convolutional neural network (NbNet) for reconstructing face images from deep templates, even under the challenging assumption of no prior knowledge about the target subject or the underlying network. By situating our approach within the broader landscape of face recognition, template security, and adversarial attacks, we aim to advance the understanding of vulnerabilities in deep face recognition systems and inform the development of more secure biometric technologies.

The reconstruction of face images from deep face templates is a research area that intersects face recognition, deep representation learning, privacy, and generative modeling. Early work in face recognition focused on designing robust feature representations under unconstrained conditions, as benchmarked by Liao et al. (2014), who highlighted the challenges of large-scale unconstrained face datasets and the importance of discriminative deep features. As deep learning became prevalent, Nair et al. (2010) demonstrated how rectified linear units (ReLU) improved the training of deep models, facilitating the learning of more expressive and robust representations.

The development of highly discriminative face templates has enabled remarkable progress in recognition performance, as evidenced by Masi et al. (2016), who questioned the need for massive datasets in achieving state-of-the-art results. Concurrently, Wolf et al. (2011) addressed face recognition in videos, proposing techniques to handle background similarity, further motivating the need for robust representations. However, the use of deep templates has raised significant privacy concerns, particularly regarding the possibility of reconstructing original face images from these compact representations.

Reconstruction from deep templates is conceptually linked to template inversion attacks, where the goal is to recover visual information from feature vectors. Mohanty et al. (2007) introduced model-based approaches for inferring face images from similarity scores and templates, laying the groundwork for later deep learning-based inversion methods. More recently, Zhmoginov et al. (2016) investigated the inversion of face embeddings using convolutional neural networks, demonstrating that it is possible to reconstruct plausible face images from deep templates, thus exposing potential vulnerabilities in current recognition systems.

The advent of generative adversarial networks (GANs) has revolutionized the field of image synthesis and inversion. Goodfellow (2016) provided a comprehensive overview of GANs, establishing their foundational principles. Radford et al. (2015) introduced deep convolutional GANs (DCGANs), which significantly improved the quality and stability of generated images and have since become a standard for generative modeling tasks, including template inversion. Training GANs remains challenging; Salimans et al. (2016) proposed improved training techniques, while Mao et al. (2016) introduced least-squares GANs to stabilize training and enhance synthesis quality.

To further improve perceptual quality, Johnson et al. (2016) proposed perceptual loss functions, which enable the generation of images that better preserve high-level features, a technique that has direct applications in face template inversion. The choice of representation and regularization is also critical; Mairal et al. (2009) developed online dictionary learning for sparse coding, which influences how templates can be structured for both recognition and inversion tasks. On the system side, efficient frameworks like MXNet, introduced by Chen et al. (2015), have facilitated scalable experimentation with deep networks for both recognition and generative tasks.

Face template inversion also has important implications for security and anti-spoofing. Liu et al. (2018) explored the design of deep models for face anti-spoofing, highlighting the potential for auxiliary supervision to improve robustness against attacks, including those enabled by template inversion. Hayat et al. (2017) proposed joint registration and representation learning, which can inadvertently influence the invertibility of deep templates by encouraging more structured representations.

In summary, the reconstruction of face images from deep templates builds upon advances in deep face recognition (Liao et al., 2014; Masi et al., 2016), adversarial generative modeling (Goodfellow, 2016; Radford et al., 2015; Mao et al., 2016), and template inversion (Mohanty et al., 2007; Zhmoginov et al., 2016), while raising new privacy and security challenges for the deployment of deep biometric systems.

prompt: Quality and Diversity Optimization: A Unifying Modular Framework
text:
The search for optimal solutions has long been a central focus in optimization and machine learning, with classical approaches such as genetic algorithms (GAs) and evolutionary strategies forming the foundation of much of the field. Early work by Goldberg et al. (1990) provided a comparative analysis of selection schemes in GAs, highlighting the importance of balancing exploration and exploitation. This balance is further complicated in multimodal or deceptive landscapes, where maintaining diversity is crucial to avoid premature convergence. To address this, a variety of niching methods have been proposed, including fitness sharing (Mahfoud, 1996) and clearing procedures (Pétrowski, 1996), which explicitly encourage the maintenance of diverse subpopulations within evolutionary algorithms.

The concept of diversity in optimization is closely linked to the notion of evolvability, as explored by Altenberg (1994), who investigated how genetic programming systems can be designed to foster the evolution of evolvability itself. This line of research has been extended by Tarapore et al. (2014), who introduced evolvability signatures to characterize generative encodings beyond standard performance benchmarks, emphasizing the importance of diversity not just in solutions, but in the capacity to generate novel and adaptive behaviors.

In parallel, the field of evolutionary robotics has provided compelling demonstrations of the value of diversity and quality in solution sets. Lipson et al. (2000) pioneered the automatic design and manufacture of robotic lifeforms, illustrating how evolutionary processes can yield a wide variety of functional morphologies. Subsequent work by Bongard et al. (2006) introduced resilient machines capable of continuous self-modeling, further underscoring the benefits of maintaining a repertoire of diverse, high-performing solutions. The challenge of transferring solutions from simulation to reality, known as the "reality gap," has been addressed by Koos et al. (2013) through the transferability approach, which explicitly considers both performance and diversity to improve real-world applicability.

Multiobjective optimization represents another major research direction where the simultaneous pursuit of quality and diversity is essential. Laumanns et al. (2002) proposed methods for combining convergence and diversity in evolutionary multiobjective optimization, laying the groundwork for algorithms that seek to approximate the entire Pareto front rather than a single optimal solution. This perspective aligns closely with the goals of quality-diversity (QD) optimization, which aims to discover a collection of diverse, high-quality solutions spanning a range of user-defined features or behaviors.

Recent advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence have further highlighted the limitations of focusing solely on performance. For example, Nguyen et al. (2014) demonstrated that deep neural networks can be easily fooled by unrecognizable images, suggesting that robustness and diversity in solution sets are critical for reliable deployment. In reinforcement learning, Kober et al. (2013) surveyed approaches in robotics that increasingly leverage diverse policy repertoires to enhance adaptability and generalization.

The emergence of QD algorithms represents a unifying framework that synthesizes these diverse research threads. Lehman et al. (2015) introduced mechanisms such as extinction events to enhance divergent search, directly addressing the need for both exploration and the preservation of high-performing solutions. Foundational texts on stochastic search and optimization, such as Hesterberg (2004) and Nowak (2007), provide the theoretical underpinnings for these developments, offering a broad perspective on the challenges and opportunities in optimizing for both quality and diversity.

Finally, the discovery of interpretable and generalizable patterns from data, as exemplified by Schmidt et al. (2009), further motivates the need for optimization frameworks that do not merely seek a single best solution, but rather a diverse set of high-quality candidates. The present work builds upon and unifies these strands by proposing a modular framework for quality and diversity optimization, aiming to provide a flexible and extensible foundation for future research in this rapidly evolving area.

## Related Work

The optimization of complex functions has long been a central concern in artificial intelligence, robotics, and engineering. Traditional approaches, such as genetic algorithms (GAs), have focused on identifying a single optimal solution or a set of Pareto-optimal solutions in the case of multiobjective optimization. Goldberg et al. (1990) provided a foundational comparative analysis of selection schemes in GAs, highlighting the trade-offs between exploration and exploitation that underpin much of evolutionary computation. Building on these foundations, research has increasingly recognized the importance of not only finding high-performing solutions but also maintaining diversity within the population to avoid premature convergence and to foster innovation (Altenberg, 1994; Laumanns et al., 2002).

The concept of diversity in optimization has been explored from multiple perspectives. In multiobjective optimization, Laumanns et al. (2002) proposed methods that explicitly combine convergence towards the Pareto front with the maintenance of diversity among solutions, ensuring a well-distributed set of trade-off solutions. Altenberg (1994) introduced the notion of evolvability in genetic programming, emphasizing the long-term benefits of maintaining diverse genotypes for adaptive potential. These early works laid the groundwork for later approaches that treat diversity as a primary objective rather than a secondary concern.

A significant shift occurred with the advent of quality-diversity (QD) algorithms, which aim to generate a collection of solutions that are both high-performing and diverse according to user-defined behavioral or phenotypic descriptors. Mouret et al. (2015) introduced the MAP-Elites algorithm, which "illuminates" the search space by mapping elites into a discretized feature space, thus providing a repertoire of diverse, high-quality solutions. Pugh et al. (2015) further articulated the QD paradigm, confronting the challenge of simultaneously optimizing for quality and diversity, and providing a unifying perspective for a range of divergent search algorithms. Lehman et al. (2015) explored mechanisms such as extinction events to enhance divergent search, while Maestre et al. (2015) and Benureau et al. (2016) investigated novelty search and behavioral diversity generation in autonomous exploration, respectively, demonstrating the practical benefits of diversity-driven approaches in robotics and reinforcement learning.

QD algorithms have found particular resonance in robotics and artificial life, where the ability to generate a repertoire of behaviors is crucial for adaptation and resilience. Bongard et al. (2006) demonstrated the value of continuous self-modeling for resilient machines, while Duarte et al. (2016) proposed EvoRBC, an evolutionary repertoire-based control method for robots with complex locomotion requirements. These approaches leverage the diversity of solutions to enable robots to adapt to new tasks or recover from damage. Kober et al. (2013) surveyed reinforcement learning in robotics, noting the growing importance of methods that can autonomously discover and exploit diverse behaviors.

The interplay between diversity, evolvability, and robustness has also been explored in the context of generative encodings and deep learning. Tarapore et al. (2014) examined evolvability signatures of generative encodings, moving beyond standard performance benchmarks to assess the capacity for innovation and adaptation. Nguyen et al. (2014, 2015) highlighted both the vulnerabilities and creative potential of deep neural networks, showing that they can be easily fooled but also harnessed as "innovation engines" for automated creativity and improved stochastic optimization.

Finally, the broader landscape of stochastic search and optimization has been surveyed by Nowak (2007), who reviewed foundational methods and their applications across estimation, simulation, and control. The emergence of QD algorithms represents a unifying trend that bridges these diverse research directions, offering modular frameworks that can be adapted to a wide range of domains and problem settings.

In summary, the proposed unifying modular framework for quality and diversity optimization builds upon a rich history of research in evolutionary computation, multiobjective optimization, divergent search, and behavioral diversity. By integrating and generalizing these approaches, it aims to provide a flexible foundation for future advances in the generation of diverse, high-quality solution sets.

## Related Work

The optimization of both quality and diversity in solution spaces has long been a central concern in evolutionary computation, machine learning, and robotics. Traditional optimization approaches have predominantly focused on maximizing a single objective or a set of objectives, often neglecting the importance of maintaining diversity among solutions. However, recent advancements highlight the crucial role of diversity in fostering robustness, adaptability, and innovation within artificial systems. This section reviews foundational and contemporary works that have shaped the landscape of quality and diversity optimization, situating our proposed unifying modular framework within this broader context.

Early research in evolutionary algorithms established the necessity of diversity preservation to prevent premature convergence and maintain exploration capabilities. Goldberg et al. (1987) introduced sharing mechanisms that allowed populations to explore multimodal landscapes effectively, laying the groundwork for subsequent niching techniques. Pétrowski (1996) further advanced this line of research by proposing the clearing procedure, a niching method that maintains diversity by limiting the number of individuals allowed within a niche, thus promoting the exploration of multiple optima.

Multi-objective optimization approaches have also grappled with the trade-off between convergence towards optimal solutions and the maintenance of diversity across the Pareto front. Laumanns et al. (2002) provided a formal framework for balancing convergence and diversity in evolutionary multi-objective optimization, which has influenced the design of many modern algorithms. Antoniou et al. (2021) offer a comprehensive overview of practical optimization algorithms, emphasizing the role of diversity maintenance in engineering applications and highlighting modular approaches to algorithm design.

Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms, a more recent development, explicitly optimize for both high-performing and diverse solutions. Lehman et al. (2011) pioneered this paradigm with novelty search and local competition, demonstrating that encouraging diversity can discover a wide array of valuable behaviors in robotic agents. Building on this, Vassiliades et al. (2016) introduced centroidal Voronoi tessellations to scale up the MAP-Elites algorithm, allowing efficient coverage of large behavior spaces. Tarapore et al. (2016) investigated how different encodings affect the performance of MAP-Elites, revealing the interplay between representation choices and the ability to generate diverse, high-quality solutions.

The study of generative encodings has further illuminated the relationship between representation, evolvability, and diversity. Tarapore et al. (2014) analyzed evolvability signatures of generative encodings, moving beyond standard performance benchmarks to assess the potential for producing novel and adaptive behaviors. Eiben et al. (2015) expanded the scope of evolutionary computation by discussing the evolution of physical artifacts ("the evolution of things"), highlighting the necessity for diversity-oriented algorithms in real-world applications.

In robotics, QD algorithms have proven effective in tackling complex control and adaptation tasks. Duarte et al. (2016) proposed EvoRBC, an evolutionary repertoire-based control framework that leverages diverse solution sets to address arbitrary locomotion complexity, while Kohl et al. (2004) employed policy gradient reinforcement learning to rapidly develop diverse quadrupedal locomotion policies. Maestre et al. (2015) employed novelty search to bootstrap interactions with objects from raw sensorimotor data, reinforcing the value of diversity-driven search in open-ended learning contexts.

Beyond evolutionary computation and robotics, the optimization of both quality and diversity has found applications in data-driven scientific discovery and information processing. Schmidt et al. (2009) introduced methods for distilling free-form natural laws from experimental data, where diversity in hypothesis generation is critical for scientific exploration. Demiris et al. (2013) explored information processing in the mirror neuron system, drawing parallels between biological diversity in behavior and artificial systems' need for varied solution repertoires.

Lastly, the theoretical underpinnings of stochastic search and optimization, as outlined by Hesterberg (2004), continue to inform the development of modular frameworks that can flexibly integrate quality and diversity objectives.

Taken collectively, these works underscore the growing recognition of diversity as a key axis of optimization, alongside quality. However, existing approaches often lack modularity and generality, motivating the need for a unifying framework that can accommodate a variety of domains, representations, and optimization strategies. Our work addresses this gap by proposing a modular architecture that systematically unifies quality and diversity optimization, building on the foundational insights and practical advancements detailed above.

## Related Work

Quantitative assessment of myocardial perfusion is a critical component in the diagnosis and management of coronary artery disease (CAD). Over the past several decades, a variety of imaging modalities and kinetic modeling approaches have been developed to enable absolute quantification of myocardial blood flow (MBF). Among these, positron emission tomography (PET) using ^15O-labeled water has emerged as the reference standard, while dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) has gained traction as a non-ionizing alternative. This section reviews the evolution of quantitative myocardial perfusion imaging, focusing on methodological advances and comparative studies across PET and MRI modalities.

### PET Imaging and Kinetic Modeling

PET imaging with ^15O-water has long been established as the gold standard for MBF quantification due to its favorable tracer kinetics and validated modeling approaches. Early foundational work by Lammertsma et al. (1992) compared tracer models for regional myocardial blood flow measurement using C^15O_2 and PET, highlighting the importance of accurate kinetic modeling in deriving physiologically meaningful parameters. Subsequent methodological advances have focused on improving the speed and robustness of parametric image generation. Chen et al. (1998) introduced a generalized linear least squares method for rapid generation of MBF parametric images with N-13 ammonia PET, while Boellaard et al. (2005) evaluated both basis function and linear least squares methods for generating parametric blood flow images using ^15O-water PET, demonstrating the trade-offs between computational efficiency and accuracy. Similarly, Lee et al. (2005) proposed a linear least-squares approach for generating regional MBF parametric images with H_2^15O dynamic PET, further streamlining the quantification process.

The clinical value of absolute MBF quantification with ^15O-water PET has been substantiated in several studies. Kajander et al. (2011) demonstrated the utility of this technique in the assessment of CAD, while Danad et al. (2014) established cutoff values and diagnostic accuracy for quantitative ^15O-H_2O PET imaging in detecting significant coronary artery disease. These studies collectively underscore the reliability and clinical relevance of PET-based MBF quantification.

### Quantitative Myocardial Perfusion MRI

DCE-MRI has emerged as a promising alternative for MBF quantification, offering high spatial resolution and the advantage of avoiding ionizing radiation. Methodological developments in MRI-based perfusion quantification have paralleled those in PET, with a focus on both model-based and model-independent approaches. Pack et al. (2008) introduced a model-independent deconvolution method for estimating myocardial perfusion from dynamic contrast-enhanced CMR, while Garpebring et al. (2009) proposed a novel estimation method using a distributed parameter model and Fourier-domain calculations to improve physiological parameter estimation.

Comparative studies have evaluated the performance of different kinetic models in MRI. Broadbent et al. (2013) compared a distributed parameter model with a Fermi function model for MBF estimation at rest and stress, and Papanastasiou et al. (2016) assessed Fermi and distributed parameter modeling against invasive reference standards, providing insights into the strengths and limitations of each approach. Biglands et al. (2015) further compared the diagnostic performance of four quantitative myocardial perfusion estimation methods in cardiac MR imaging, highlighting the variability in accuracy and reproducibility across techniques.

### Multimodality Comparisons and Clinical Validation

Direct comparisons between PET and MRI modalities have been instrumental in validating the clinical utility of DCE-MRI for MBF quantification. Fritz-Hansen et al. (2008) compared MRI-measured myocardial perfusion reserve in healthy humans with PET, demonstrating comparable results and supporting the use of MRI as a viable alternative. Morton et al. (2012) extended this comparison to patients with CAD, finding good agreement between cardiovascular magnetic resonance and PET for absolute myocardial perfusion quantification. Huber et al. (2012) evaluated both semiquantitative and quantitative MRI perfusion against coronary angiography and fractional flow reserve, further establishing the diagnostic value of MRI-based approaches.

### Statistical Evaluation and Diagnostic Performance

The assessment of diagnostic performance in myocardial perfusion imaging often relies on receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. DeLong et al. (1988) provided a nonparametric approach for comparing the areas under two or more correlated ROC curves, a method widely adopted in subsequent studies to evaluate and compare the diagnostic accuracy of different imaging modalities and quantification techniques.

### Summary

In summary, the field of quantitative myocardial perfusion imaging has seen significant methodological advancements in both PET and MRI modalities. PET with ^15O-water remains the reference standard, but DCE-MRI has demonstrated comparable diagnostic performance in multiple studies. Ongoing research continues to refine kinetic modeling approaches and validate MRI-based quantification against established PET techniques, with the ultimate goal of improving the noninvasive assessment of myocardial perfusion in clinical practice.

### Quantitative Myocardial Perfusion with DCE-MRI

DCE-MRI has emerged as a powerful noninvasive tool for myocardial perfusion assessment, offering high spatial resolution and the ability to assess both perfusion and tissue characterization in a single examination. Quantitative CMR techniques have evolved from semi-quantitative indices to model-based absolute flow estimation. Pack et al. In summary, the literature demonstrates that both [15O]H2O PET and DCE-CMR provide robust frameworks for quantitative myocardial perfusion assessment. Technical advances in tracer kinetics modeling, automation, and image analysis have enabled accurate, reproducible, and clinically meaningful MBF quantification. Direct comparative studies and meta-analyses consistently highlight the value of quantitative approaches, with PET serving as the reference standard and CMR offering a versatile, radiation-free alternative. The integration of these modalities and their quantitative metrics forms the basis for contemporary multimodality assessment of myocardial perfusion, driving ongoing innovation and clinical translation in cardiovascular imaging.

Conversational AI research has also focused on the personalization and contextualization of dialogue agents. Zhang et al. (2018) investigated methods for personalizing dialogue systems, enabling agents to maintain consistent personas and engage in more natural interactions. El-Assady et al. As language models have grown in scale and capability, concerns regarding interpretability, robustness, and bias have become increasingly prominent. Doshi-Velez et al. (2017) called for a rigorous science of interpretable machine learning, emphasizing the need for transparency in model decision-making. Jin et al. (2019) evaluated the robustness of BERT-based models to adversarial attacks, while Bender et al. (2018) proposed data statements as a means to mitigate system bias and improve scientific rigor in NLP research. Bender et al. Recent work has also explored the application of large language models to specialized domains and tasks. Moradi et al. (2020) leveraged deep contextualized embeddings for biomedical text summarization, demonstrating the adaptability of pre-trained models to domain-specific challenges. Chen et al. (2021) evaluated the performance of large language models trained on code, highlighting their potential for tasks beyond natural language, such as program synthesis and code completion.

Collectively, these lines of research provide the methodological and conceptual foundation for the development and evaluation of ChatGPT. This paper situates itself within this landscape by offering a preliminary review of ChatGPT’s training process, core functionalities, and the broader implications of large-scale conversational AI models.

## Related Work

The rapid evolution of natural language processing (NLP) has been driven by advances in neural architectures, large-scale pre-training, and the increasing availability of conversational datasets. Early work in neural machine translation, such as Wu et al. (2016) and the development of open-source toolkits like OpenNMT (Klein et al., 2017), laid the groundwork for sequence-to-sequence modeling and the adoption of deep learning in language tasks. The introduction of the Transformer architecture by Vaswani et al. (2017) marked a pivotal shift, enabling models to capture long-range dependencies through self-attention mechanisms and forming the backbone of subsequent large-scale language models.

Building on these foundations, pre-trained language models such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019) demonstrated the effectiveness of unsupervised pre-training followed by task-specific fine-tuning, significantly improving performance across a range of NLP benchmarks. Howard et al. (2018) further contributed to this paradigm with universal language model fine-tuning, emphasizing the transferability of pre-trained representations. These advances have been instrumental in enabling models like ChatGPT to generate coherent and contextually appropriate responses in open-domain conversations.

Conversational AI has seen notable progress with the emergence of large-scale generative models. Zhang et al. (2019) introduced DIALOGPT, which leveraged large-scale pre-training for conversational response generation, highlighting the importance of data scale and model capacity in dialogue systems. Brown et al. (2020) extended this approach with GPT-3, demonstrating few-shot learning capabilities and further blurring the line between human and machine-generated text. The evaluation of large language models on specialized domains, such as code (Chen et al., 2021), underscores the versatility and generalization potential of these architectures.

Beyond model architectures and training paradigms, the NLP community has increasingly focused on the ethical, social, and environmental implications of large language models. Bender et al. (2018) advocated for the use of data statements to mitigate system bias and improve scientific transparency, while Strubell et al. (2019) raised concerns about the energy consumption and policy considerations associated with deep learning at scale. Bender et al. (2020) further critiqued the limitations of current models in achieving true natural language understanding, emphasizing the distinction between form and meaning.

In parallel, research has explored the visualization and analysis of conversational data (El-Assady et al., 2016), robustness in text detection (Ch’ng et al., 2019), and multilingual modeling (Wang et al., 2019), each contributing to the broader ecosystem in which models like ChatGPT are developed and evaluated. Collectively, these works provide the methodological and conceptual context for the present review, situating ChatGPT within ongoing efforts to advance conversational AI while addressing the attendant challenges of scale, bias, and interpretability.

In finance, Dowling et al. (2023) explored the capabilities of ChatGPT for research and data analysis, humorously referring to its limitations as the "Bananarama Conjecture." The study illustrated both the potential and pitfalls of relying on large language models for financial analysis, particularly with respect to accuracy and trustworthiness.

The broader trajectory of neural network-based language models is rooted in earlier foundational work. Wu et al. (2016) introduced Google's Neural Machine Translation System, marking a significant milestone in bridging the gap between human and machine translation. Devlin et al. The interpretability of these complex models remains a critical concern, as emphasized by Doshi-Velez et al. (2017), who called for a rigorous science of interpretable machine learning to foster trust and accountability.

Early in the pandemic, the need for scalable and accurate diagnostic solutions was highlighted by Lang (2020), who emphasized the importance of closing research gaps in detection and care. Manual interpretation of chest X-rays, while effective, is time-consuming and subject to inter-reader variability, as demonstrated by Cozzi et al. (2020), who evaluated radiologists’ real-world performance during the pandemic. This has motivated the development of computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems to assist clinicians and improve diagnostic throughput.

Deep learning, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), has become the dominant methodology for automated medical image analysis. Several studies have explored CNN-based approaches for COVID-19 detection from chest X-rays. Al-antari et al. (2020) proposed a fast deep learning CAD system specifically tailored for COVID-19 diagnosis using digital chest X-ray images, demonstrating the potential for rapid and accurate screening. Similarly, Qi et al. (2020) enhanced COVID-19 diagnosis by extracting phase features from chest X-ray images and employing CNNs, while Oh et al. (2020) addressed the challenge of limited training data by developing deep learning models capable of extracting COVID-19 features from small datasets. The availability of curated datasets, such as the one provided by Sait et al. (2020), has further facilitated the development and benchmarking of these deep learning models.

Beyond X-rays, other imaging modalities have also been explored. Li et al. (2020) introduced a stacked-autoencoder-based model for COVID-19 diagnosis using CT images, highlighting the versatility of deep learning architectures in handling different types of medical data. More broadly, Muhammad et al. (2020) surveyed the application of deep learning for various medical image classification tasks, including brain tumor detection, underscoring the generalizability of these techniques across healthcare domains.

While CNNs have dominated medical image analysis, recent advances in transformer architectures have begun to influence the field. Originally developed for natural language processing, as exemplified by BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and GPT (Radford et al., 2019), transformers have demonstrated strong performance in vision tasks due to their ability to model long-range dependencies. Devaraj (2019) discussed the emergence of transform-based paradigms in medical image compression, foreshadowing the broader adoption of transformer models in medical imaging. The Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture, in particular, has shown promise for image classification tasks, motivating its application to COVID-19 detection.

The effectiveness of deep learning models, including transformers, is often enhanced by regularization and normalization techniques. L2 regularization, as described by Cortes et al. (2009), helps prevent overfitting in kernel-based learning, while batch normalization (Ioffe et al., 2015) accelerates training and improves generalization in deep networks. Activation functions such as Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs) (Hendrycks et al., 2016) have also contributed to improved model performance. Additionally, label smoothing, investigated by Müller et al. (2019), has been shown to enhance generalization and calibration in classification tasks.

In summary, the intersection of deep learning, medical imaging, and transformer-based architectures represents a promising direction for automated COVID-19 detection. The proposed Vision Transformer-based pipeline builds upon these advances, aiming to deliver interpretable and accurate diagnostic support for healthcare professionals.

Accountability has long been recognized as a foundational concept in governance, public administration, and democratic theory. Early work by Sinclair (1995) highlighted the multifaceted and context-dependent nature of accountability, describing it as a "chameleon" that adapts to different institutional and discursive settings. Mulgan (2003) further developed this perspective, analyzing how modern democracies operationalize accountability to hold power to account, while Grant et al. (2005) extended the discussion to the international arena, examining mechanisms for preventing abuses of power in world politics. Schmitter et al. (2008) contributed to this foundational literature by clarifying the role of accountability within democratic systems, emphasizing its importance for legitimacy and effective governance.

Within the academic discourse, scholars have debated the conceptual boundaries and mechanisms of accountability. Bovens (2010) distinguished between accountability as a virtue—an ethical quality of actors—and as a mechanism—a set of institutional practices for oversight and answerability. Olsen (2017) addressed the persistent ambiguity in accountability’s definition and its political implications, echoing Sinclair’s (1995) observation of its protean character. These works collectively underscore the need for greater conceptual clarity, a gap that the present paper seeks to address by offering a structured definition of accountability in AI.

The rise of artificial intelligence has prompted a growing body of research on how traditional notions of accountability translate to sociotechnical systems. Floridi (2012) introduced the idea of "distributed morality," arguing that responsibility and accountability in information societies are often shared across networks of human and non-human agents. This insight is particularly salient for AI, where agency and decision-making are frequently distributed. Busuioc (2020) specifically examined the challenges of holding algorithms to account, identifying institutional and technical barriers to effective oversight. Zech (2021) explored the legal dimensions of AI accountability, focusing on liability and public policy considerations, while Theodorou et al. (2020) advocated for ethical and socio-legal governance frameworks that can accommodate the unique characteristics of AI systems.

Recent work has also focused on operationalizing accountability in AI through principles, design, and practice. Fjeld et al. (2020) mapped the emerging consensus around ethical and rights-based principles for AI, highlighting accountability as a recurring theme across frameworks. Desouza et al. (2020) examined the practical challenges of designing, developing, and deploying AI in the public sector, emphasizing the need for robust accountability mechanisms throughout the system lifecycle. Barclay et al. (2021) proposed a taxonomy of roles, requirements, and responsibilities necessary for trustworthy AI, while Srinivasan et al. (2021) investigated the role of empathy in fostering AI accountability, suggesting that human-centered values must inform technical and organizational processes.

Finally, the relationship between automation, human oversight, and accountability has been explored in the context of system design and human factors. Endsley et al. (1999) studied how varying levels of automation affect human performance, situation awareness, and workload, findings that have direct implications for the allocation of accountability in AI-enabled environments.

In summary, the literature reveals both the complexity and the urgency of clarifying accountability in the context of AI. While prior work has mapped the conceptual terrain and identified key challenges, there remains a need for a systematic framework that articulates the conditions and features of accountability specific to AI systems. This paper contributes to the field by addressing this gap, offering a nuanced definition and an architecture for understanding and implementing accountability in artificial intelligence.

## Related Work

The concept of accountability has deep roots in political science, governance, and organizational theory, yet its application to artificial intelligence (AI) is a relatively recent and rapidly evolving area of study. Foundational scholarship on accountability, such as Bovens (2007), provides a conceptual framework distinguishing between accountability as a virtue and as a mechanism, emphasizing the importance of answerability and the relationship between actors and forums. Lindberg (2013) further refines this by mapping the core concept and subtypes of accountability, which helps clarify the multiplicity of meanings and applications across contexts. These works underpin contemporary debates about how to translate accountability into the technological domain.

In the AI context, Busuioc (2020) explores the specific challenges of holding algorithms to account, highlighting issues of opacity, complexity, and the shifting of responsibility between human and automated agents. This aligns with Floridi (2016), who addresses the problem of "faultless responsibility"—the difficulty of attributing moral responsibility in distributed systems where multiple actors and autonomous technologies interact. Such conceptual challenges are compounded by socio-political factors, as noted by Rubenstein (2007), who discusses the asymmetries of power and inequality that can affect the efficacy of accountability structures.

Binns (2017) discusses algorithmic accountability in relation to public reason, emphasizing the need for transparency and justification of algorithmic decisions, particularly when they affect individuals and public interests. Olsen (2017) adds that ambiguity is an inherent feature of accountability politics, which can be exacerbated in technological settings due to complex and contested attributions of responsibility. These considerations are central to debates about what constitutes effective accountability in AI.

From an organizational perspective, Bovens (2010) distinguishes between accountability as a virtue—emphasizing ethical conduct—and as a mechanism—focusing on formal procedures and processes. This distinction is especially relevant for AI, where both ethical norms and concrete mechanisms, such as audits or impact assessments, are necessary for meaningful accountability. Grant et al. (2005) investigate how accountability can curb abuses of power in global politics, providing insights into the broader societal importance of accountability mechanisms, which can be analogously applied to the governance of AI.

The design and operation of AI systems also pose unique challenges for accountability. Baxter et al. (2011) discuss the complexities of socio-technical systems, underscoring the necessity for design methods that incorporate human factors and system-level thinking. Endsley et al. (1999) examine how different levels of automation affect human performance, situation awareness, and workload, illustrating the intricate interplay between automated systems and their human operators—an area where accountability can become blurred.

Transparency and explainability are frequently cited as prerequisites for AI accountability. Gilpin et al. (2018) provide an overview of interpretability in machine learning, surveying technical methods for making AI systems more understandable, while Miller (2017) advocates for explanation in AI, drawing on insights from social sciences to inform the design of systems that can provide meaningful justifications for their outputs. Ehsan et al. (2021) extend this discussion by introducing the concept of social transparency, which emphasizes the importance of making AI systems' reasoning and decision-making processes accessible to a broad range of stakeholders.

Finally, Fjeld et al. (2020) map the emerging consensus around ethical and rights-based principles for AI, noting that accountability is a recurring theme across national and international guidelines. This highlights the growing recognition that robust accountability mechanisms are both a normative requirement and a practical necessity for trustworthy and responsible AI.

Collectively, these works demonstrate that accountability in AI is a multidimensional concept, involving ethical, technical, organizational, and societal dimensions. Addressing these challenges requires interdisciplinary approaches that draw from established theories of accountability and adapt them to the unique characteristics of artificial intelligence systems.

### Visual Question Answering and Multimodal Fusion

Visual Question Answering (VQA) has emerged as a pivotal task at the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing, aiming to enable machines to answer natural language questions about visual content. Early approaches to VQA focused on effective multimodal fusion strategies to combine visual and textual information. For instance, Fukui et al. (2016) introduced Multimodal Compact Bilinear Pooling, which efficiently captures interactions between image and question features, while Arevalo et al. (2017) proposed Gated Multimodal Units to dynamically control the flow of information from different modalities. More recently, relational reasoning and attention mechanisms have been leveraged to further enhance feature fusion, as demonstrated by Zhang et al. (2020), who combined relational reasoning with attention to improve VQA performance. Comprehensive reviews such as Manmadhan et al. (2020) provide an overview of the evolution and state-of-the-art in VQA, highlighting the importance of robust multimodal integration.

### Visual Grounding and Localization in VQA

A key limitation of traditional VQA systems is their inability to visually ground answers, i.e., to localize the image regions relevant to a given question. Visual grounding methods address this by linking textual queries to specific visual regions. Deng et al. (2020) proposed an accumulated attention mechanism to improve visual grounding, while Mani et al. (2020) introduced the "Point and Ask" paradigm, explicitly incorporating pointing to enhance interpretability in VQA. These approaches underscore the growing emphasis on explainability and transparency in VQA systems, particularly in high-stakes domains such as medicine.

### Medical VQA and Domain-Specific Challenges

The application of VQA to medical imaging introduces unique challenges, including the need for domain-specific knowledge and the requirement for high reliability. Vu et al. (2020) addressed these challenges by proposing a question-centric model tailored for medical VQA, demonstrating improved performance on clinical datasets. However, most existing medical VQA models still lack robust mechanisms for visual localization, limiting their utility in clinical decision support and education.

### Object Detection and Localization Techniques

Advances in object detection have significantly influenced visual grounding and VQA. Ren et al. (2015) introduced Faster R-CNN, a seminal framework for real-time object detection using region proposal networks, while Lin et al. (2017) proposed focal loss to address class imbalance in dense detection tasks. More recently, transformer-based architectures such as DETR (Carion et al., 2020) have enabled end-to-end object detection with improved localization accuracy. For bounding box regression, Rezatofighi et al. (2019) introduced the Generalized Intersection Over Union (GIoU) metric, providing a more robust loss function for localization tasks. These advances form the backbone of many visual grounding and VQA systems.

### Representation Learning and Contrastive Methods

Learning robust visual representations is critical for both VQA and visual grounding. Chen et al. (2020) introduced a simple yet effective framework for contrastive learning, which has become a cornerstone for self-supervised visual representation learning. In the context of multimodal tasks, contrastive objectives can help align visual and textual modalities, improving both robustness and generalization.

### Adversarial Robustness and Calibration

Robustness to adversarial examples and model calibration are increasingly important in safety-critical applications such as robotic surgery. Goodfellow et al. (2014) highlighted the vulnerability of deep networks to adversarial perturbations, motivating research into adversarial training and robust learning objectives. Kendall et al. (2017) explored multi-task learning with uncertainty-based loss weighting, providing a principled approach to balancing competing objectives and improving model calibration.

### Language Understanding in VQA

The integration of advanced language models has further propelled progress in VQA. Devlin et al. (2019) introduced BERT, a deep bidirectional transformer that has set new benchmarks in language understanding and has been widely adopted for question encoding in VQA pipelines.

### Summary

In summary, the intersection of VQA, visual grounding, robust representation learning, and adversarial robustness forms the foundation for recent advances in medical and surgical VQA. However, the challenge of providing calibrated, robust, and visually localized answers in the context of robotic surgery remains largely unaddressed. Our work builds upon these foundational advances, introducing adversarial contrastive learning and explicit visual localization to bridge this critical gap.

Despite these advances, standard VQA models often lack the ability to localize the visual evidence supporting their answers, which is particularly critical in high-stakes domains such as medicine. Loss functions such as focal loss (Lin et al., 2017) and generalized intersection over union (Rezatofighi et al., 2019) have been proposed to enhance detection accuracy and localization, while multi-task learning strategies (Kendall et al., 2017) offer principled approaches to balancing competing objectives.

Our work builds upon these foundations by introducing an adversarial contrastive learning framework for surgical visual question-localized answering (VQLA), aiming to deliver calibrated and robust performance in robotic surgery. ### Visual Question Answering in Medical and Surgical Domains

VQA has undergone rapid progress, especially with the rise of deep learning and multimodal transformers. In the medical domain, Sharma et al. The clinical relevance of VQA systems is further underscored by Lau et al. (2018), who curated Descriptor, a dataset of real-world visual questions and answers in radiology, thus catalyzing research grounded in authentic clinical scenarios.

Despite these advances, medical VQA systems often face challenges related to dataset bias, limited training samples, and the need for robust and calibrated predictions under real-world perturbations—a gap that motivates the development of new architectures such as Surgical-VQLA++.

### Robustness and Calibration in Deep Learning

Robustness to input corruptions and model calibration are crucial in safety-critical applications like robotic surgery. Hendrycks et al. (2019) systematically benchmarked neural network robustness to common corruptions and perturbations, establishing protocols that have inspired robustness studies in the medical imaging space. Hoque et al. (2023) specifically evaluated robustness stress testing in medical image classification, demonstrating how even state-of-the-art networks can struggle under realistic noise and distribution shifts. These findings highlight the necessity for VQA models in surgery to be resilient and trustworthy, motivating the integration of adversarial and contrastive learning strategies for enhanced robustness and calibration.

### Visual Grounding and Localization

Precise identification of answer-relevant image regions is fundamental for question-localized answering. Deng et al. (2020) proposed an accumulated attention mechanism for visual grounding, effectively aligning textual queries with visual evidence. Similarly, Li et al. (2022) addressed the temporal grounding of answers in instructional videos, a task closely related to the spatiotemporal reasoning required in surgical VQA. Khan et al. (2021) introduced weakly-supervised grounded VQA using capsules, which enables localization of answer-supporting regions even with limited annotation, a scenario often encountered in surgical datasets.

The need for explainable and interpretable localization in medical contexts has been further addressed by Parelli et al. (2023), who introduced reasoning supervision to VQA models, improving both performance and transparency. These advances underpin the design of models like Surgical-VQLA++, which seek to provide both accurate answers and evidence localization in a unified, interpretable framework.

### Multimodal and Cross-Modal Learning

Integrating visual and linguistic modalities has become central to VQA research. Yu et al. (2019) introduced deep modular co-attention networks, demonstrating the effectiveness of joint attention mechanisms for VQA. Gouthaman et al. (2020) tackled language biases by proposing visually-grounded question encoders, which reduce the model’s reliance on superficial textual cues—a critical consideration for generalizing to out-of-distribution questions in surgery.

Uppal et al. (2022) provided a comprehensive review of multimodal research in vision and language, highlighting emerging trends such as contrastive learning and cross-modal pretraining, which are directly relevant to the adversarial contrastive learning formulation of Surgical-VQLA++. These approaches facilitate better alignment between modalities, improving both robustness and localization.

### Medical Image Analysis and Surgical Applications

The unique visual characteristics of surgical imagery introduce additional challenges. Wu et al. (2022) leveraged contextual transformer-based CNNs for complex anatomical structure extraction in CT images, showcasing the potential of hybrid architectures for capturing fine-grained details in medical images. In the surgical context, Chen et al. (2024) proposed LighTDiff, a diffusion-based technique for enhancing low-light endoscopic images—a frequent issue in surgery that can affect downstream VQA performance.

Finally, the availability of large-scale datasets like ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) has been instrumental in pretraining visual backbones, but domain adaptation remains essential for bridging the gap between natural and surgical images.

### Summary

In summary, prior work has established key building blocks for robust, interpretable, and localized VQA in medical and surgical domains. However, the integration of adversarial contrastive learning for simultaneous robustness, calibration, and precise answer localization in robotic surgery remains underexplored. Surgical-VQLA++ aims to bridge these gaps by drawing on insights from robustness, grounding, multimodal alignment, and surgical image enhancement to deliver reliable and explainable visual question-localized answering tailored for the operating room.

**Related Work**

Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) has long been a critical area of research, with early statistical approaches such as ARIMA-based residual analysis (Box et al., 1970) laying the groundwork for subsequent developments. Traditional methods often rely on explicit modeling of normal patterns and statistical deviations, but their effectiveness is limited in complex, high-dimensional, or non-stationary settings.

With the advent of deep learning, unsupervised and self-supervised representation learning methods have become increasingly prominent. Autoencoder-based approaches, such as those proposed by Sakurada et al. (2014) and further extended by Zong et al. (2018), leverage reconstruction errors to identify anomalies, while Park et al. (2017) introduced variational autoencoders for multimodal anomaly detection in robotics. Similarly, Zhang et al. (2018) explored deep neural networks for unsupervised anomaly detection and diagnosis in multivariate time series, highlighting the potential of deep architectures to capture complex temporal dependencies. Generative models, including MAD-GAN (Li et al., 2019), have also been employed to model the distribution of normal time series and detect deviations, offering improved flexibility over traditional methods.

Representation learning for time series has also been explored from the perspective of transferability and clustering. Malhotra et al. (2017) introduced TimeNet, a pre-trained deep recurrent neural network for time series classification, demonstrating the utility of learned representations across tasks. Lei et al. (2017) focused on similarity-preserving representation learning for time series clustering, while Wu et al. (2018) proposed Random Warping Series as a random features method for time-series embedding. Bianchi et al. (2019) addressed the challenge of missing data in multivariate time series, proposing methods for robust representation learning in the presence of incomplete observations.

Recent advances in contrastive and self-supervised learning have further enriched the landscape. Milbich et al. (2019) demonstrated the effectiveness of unsupervised representation learning by discovering reliable relations in images, inspiring analogous approaches in the time series domain. Outlier exposure, as introduced by Hendrycks et al. (2018), leverages auxiliary data to improve deep anomaly detection, while Domingues et al. (2018) provided a comprehensive evaluation of outlier detection algorithms, underscoring the need for robust and generalizable methods.

In industrial and real-world settings, the challenge of limited labeled data is particularly acute. Canizo et al. (2019) proposed a multi-head CNN-RNN architecture for multi-time series anomaly detection in industrial applications, and Mathur et al. (2016) introduced the SWaT testbed to facilitate research and benchmarking in industrial control system security. These works highlight the importance of scalable, label-efficient approaches for practical anomaly detection.

Despite these advances, many existing methods tightly define the boundary of normality, often resulting in high false positive rates and limited generalization. The proposed CARLA framework builds upon these foundations by introducing a self-supervised contrastive representation learning approach tailored for time series anomaly detection, aiming to address the limitations of prior work in terms of generalization and robustness to slight deviations from normal patterns.

prompt: CARLA: Self-supervised contrastive representation learning for time series anomaly detection
text:
## Related Work

Time series anomaly detection has been an active research area, with methods evolving from traditional statistical techniques to modern deep learning-based approaches. Early efforts often relied on statistical models and signal processing techniques, such as trend elimination using the Hodrick-Prescott filter (Phillips et al., 2020), but these methods struggled to capture complex temporal dependencies and non-linearities in real-world data.

The advent of deep learning has led to a surge in methods leveraging neural networks for representation learning and anomaly detection. Bianchi et al. (2019) proposed an approach for learning representations of multivariate time series, particularly addressing the challenge of missing data. Generative models such as GANs and VAEs have also been explored for anomaly detection, with Li et al. (2019) introducing MAD-GAN for multivariate time series and Niu et al. (2020) presenting an LSTM-based VAE-GAN framework. While these methods show promise, they often require careful training and can be sensitive to hyperparameters.

Recently, there has been growing interest in contrastive and self-supervised learning to learn powerful representations without requiring labeled data. Contrastive learning methods, initially popularized in the visual and textual domains (Caron et al., 2020; Giorgi et al., 2020), have demonstrated the ability to capture meaningful features by maximizing agreement between augmented views of the same instance. In the context of time series, Tonekaboni et al. (2021) introduced temporal neighborhood coding for unsupervised representation learning, and Yue et al. (2021) proposed TS2Vec, which learns universal representations applicable across tasks. These approaches underline the potential of self-supervised learning for extracting informative features from time series data.

For anomaly detection, several works have tailored deep learning architectures specifically for time series. Su et al. (2019) developed a stochastic recurrent neural network for robust multivariate anomaly detection, while Chen et al. (2021) introduced DAEMON, an unsupervised framework that also provides interpretability. The transformer architecture has also been adapted for time series, with Xu et al. (2021) proposing the Anomaly Transformer to identify anomalies via association discrepancy. Additionally, Xu et al. (2022) presented a calibrated one-class classification method for unsupervised detection, emphasizing the importance of calibration in practical deployment.

Comprehensive evaluations of anomaly detection methods reveal that performance varies significantly across datasets and scenarios (Domingues et al., 2018; Darban et al., 2022). Audibert et al. (2022) question whether deep neural networks inherently contribute to multivariate time series anomaly detection, suggesting that the choice of representation and learning strategy is critical.

Despite these advances, there remains a gap in effectively leveraging self-supervised contrastive learning specifically for anomaly detection in time series. Existing methods either focus on representation learning or anomaly detection, but few integrate both in a unified, self-supervised framework. CARLA addresses this gap by employing contrastive representation learning tailored to time series, demonstrating improved anomaly detection performance without reliance on labeled data.

text:
## Related Work

Multimodal machine learning has seen significant advances in recent years, driven by the need to integrate information from diverse sources such as images, text, and audio. Foundational datasets and benchmarks, such as Food-101 (Bossard et al., 2014), MIMIC-CXR (Johnson et al., 2019), and MedMNIST v2 (Yang et al., 2021), have enabled the development and evaluation of models across a range of domains, including healthcare and content moderation. These resources have highlighted both the potential and the challenges of multimodal learning, particularly in real-world settings where data may be scarce or incomplete.

A central challenge in multimodal learning is the presence of missing modalities, which can arise due to sensor failures, privacy concerns, or the high cost of data acquisition. Early work in this area, such as Mazurowski et al. (2008), examined the impact of imbalanced and incomplete datasets on medical decision-making, underscoring the importance of robust methods for handling missing data. More recently, Zeng et al. (2022) proposed tag-assisted approaches for multimodal sentiment analysis under uncertain missing modalities, while Wang et al. (2019) systematically analyzed the difficulties in training multimodal classification networks, including the effects of missing or noisy modalities. These studies collectively emphasize the need for models that can gracefully handle incomplete input, especially in high-stakes applications like healthcare.

The low-data regime presents an additional layer of difficulty, as many multimodal tasks suffer from limited annotated samples. Jin et al. (2022) addressed this issue through prototypical fine-tuning, aiming for robust performance across varying data sizes. Few-shot and in-context learning approaches have also gained traction as promising solutions. Tsimpoukelli et al. (2021) demonstrated the potential of frozen language models for multimodal few-shot learning, while Alayrac et al. (2022) introduced Flamingo, a visual language model capable of few-shot adaptation to new tasks. Wang et al. (2022) further explored in-context visual learning, showing that models can generalize to new visual tasks with minimal supervision. These works collectively suggest that leveraging context and retrieval can mitigate the challenges posed by data scarcity.

Retrieval-augmented models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for both unimodal and multimodal tasks. Borgeaud et al. (2021) showed that language models can be significantly improved by retrieving relevant information from large external corpora. In the multimodal domain, retrieval-based strategies have been used to enhance representation learning and downstream performance, as seen in Li et al. (2021), who proposed aligning vision and language representations before fusion. Gupta et al. (2022) explored compositional visual reasoning without additional training, further highlighting the flexibility of retrieval-augmented approaches.

Large-scale pretraining and contrastive learning have also played a pivotal role in advancing multimodal models. Radford et al. (2021) introduced CLIP, which learns transferable visual representations from natural language supervision, enabling robust zero-shot and few-shot performance. Kiela et al. (2020) leveraged such models in the Hateful Memes Challenge, demonstrating the importance of joint vision-language understanding for complex real-world tasks.

Despite these advances, the intersection of missing modalities and data scarcity remains underexplored. Existing methods often address either missing data or low-data regimes in isolation, but not their combination. Our work builds upon these foundations by proposing a retrieval-augmented in-context learning framework that simultaneously addresses both challenges, enabling robust multimodal learning even when both modalities and labeled samples are limited. This approach is particularly relevant for practical applications where collecting comprehensive, fully-annotated multimodal datasets is infeasible.
