## Related Work

Multimodal machine learning has seen rapid progress in recent years, driven by the availability of large-scale datasets and advances in model architectures. Foundational datasets such as MIMIC-CXR (Johnson et al., 2019) and the Hateful Memes Challenge (Kiela et al., 2020) have enabled research into complex tasks that require integrating information from multiple modalities, such as medical image interpretation and multimodal hate speech detection. However, real-world applications often face the challenge of missing modalities, where not all data sources are available for every instance.

### Multimodal Learning and Missing Modalities

Early work in multimodal learning focused on developing architectures capable of fusing information from different modalities, with an emphasis on robust representation learning (Li et al., 2021; Radford et al., 2021). Li et al. (2021) proposed momentum distillation to align vision and language representations before fusion, while Radford et al. (2021) demonstrated the effectiveness of large-scale contrastive pretraining for learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision. Despite these advances, Wang et al. (2019) highlighted the inherent difficulties in training multimodal classification networks, particularly when modalities are missing or noisy.

The robustness of multimodal models to missing modalities has become an active area of research. Ma et al. (2022) systematically evaluated the resilience of multimodal transformers under missing modality conditions, revealing significant performance drops and motivating the need for more robust approaches. Zeng et al. (2022) addressed this challenge by introducing tag-assisted methods for sentiment analysis, which leverage auxiliary information to mitigate the impact of uncertain or missing modalities.

### Few-Shot and Low-Data Regimes

The scarcity of labeled data is another major obstacle in multimodal learning, especially in domains where data collection is expensive or privacy-sensitive. Few-shot learning techniques, popularized by Brown et al. (2020) through the demonstration of in-context learning in large language models, have inspired similar approaches in the multimodal domain. Tsimpoukelli et al. (2021) explored multimodal few-shot learning by leveraging frozen language models, showing that language models can serve as effective interfaces for integrating visual information with minimal supervision. Jin et al. (2022) proposed prototypical fine-tuning to improve robustness across varying data sizes, further addressing the challenges posed by limited data availability.

### In-Context and Retrieval-Augmented Learning

Recent advances in in-context learning and retrieval-augmented models have opened new avenues for addressing both missing modalities and data scarcity. Borgeaud et al. (2021) demonstrated that augmenting language models with retrieval from large external corpora can significantly enhance performance, particularly in low-resource settings. Hao et al. (2022) further argued for the versatility of language models as general-purpose interfaces, capable of adapting to a wide range of tasks through in-context examples. In the visual domain, Wang et al. (2022) introduced a generalist painter model for in-context visual learning, while Bar et al. (2022) and Gupta et al. (2022) explored visual prompting and compositional reasoning without additional training, respectively.

### Bridging Modalities and Data Regimes

Despite these advances, the intersection of missing modalities and low-data regimes remains underexplored. While prior work has addressed each challenge in isolation—robustness to missing modalities (Ma et al., 2022; Zeng et al., 2022) and few-shot multimodal learning (Tsimpoukelli et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2022)—there is limited research on unified approaches that tackle both simultaneously. Our work builds on these foundations by proposing a retrieval-augmented in-context learning framework that leverages external knowledge to compensate for missing modalities and limited labeled data, thus addressing a critical gap in the current literature.

text:
## Related Work

Multimodal learning, which integrates information from diverse sources such as text, vision, and audio, has demonstrated remarkable success in numerous applications. However, the challenges of missing modalities and data scarcity remain significant barriers to deploying these models in real-world scenarios. Recent research has endeavored to address these limitations through innovations in model architectures, pretraining strategies, and learning paradigms.

### Multimodal Fusion and Representation Learning

Early work in multimodal learning focused on developing effective fusion techniques to integrate information from different modalities. Zadeh et al. (2018) introduced dynamic fusion graphs to interpret and analyze multimodal language data, highlighting the importance of flexible architectures for handling heterogeneous signals. More recently, Li et al. (2021) proposed momentum distillation to improve the alignment and fusion of vision and language representations, demonstrating benefits in downstream tasks. Kim et al. (2021) further advanced the field by developing ViLT, a transformer-based model that dispenses with convolutional or region-based supervision, simplifying the fusion process while maintaining competitive performance.

### Pretraining and Scaling Multimodal Models

Pretraining large-scale models on multimodal data has emerged as a dominant strategy for enhancing generalization and transferability. Radford et al. (2021) demonstrated that training on paired image-text data can yield highly transferable visual representations, a finding extended by Lin et al. (2023), who investigated pretraining strategies specifically for visual-language models and underscored the importance of careful dataset selection. Alayrac et al. (2022) introduced Flamingo, a visual-language model capable of few-shot learning, which excels even when task-specific data is scarce. Tsimpoukelli et al. (2021) showed that freezing large language models and conditioning them with multimodal information enables effective few-shot learning, further highlighting the potential of in-context learning paradigms.

### In-Context Learning and Prompting

In-context learning (ICL) has recently garnered attention as a means for large models to generalize from limited examples presented at inference time. Wei et al. (2022) demonstrated that chain-of-thought prompting can elicit sophisticated reasoning capabilities in language models, while Baldassini et al. (2024) provided an analysis of the mechanisms that drive multimodal ICL, emphasizing the importance of cross-modal retrieval and example selection. Koh et al. (2023) explored grounding language models to images for multimodal generation, suggesting that carefully designed prompts can bridge modality gaps even when some modalities are missing.

### Missing Modalities and Data Scarcity

Handling incomplete data is especially pertinent in real-world multimodal applications. Ding et al. (2025) proposed a complementary recovering approach for incomplete multimodal learning, leveraging available modalities to reconstruct missing information and improve overall performance. Similarly, Liu et al. (2023) addressed uncertain missing modalities in sentiment analysis by translating between modalities, thus mitigating the impact of absent data. The challenge of data scarcity has also been reviewed comprehensively in the context of language processing by Hedderich et al. (2020), who surveyed strategies for low-resource scenarios, many of which are applicable to multimodal settings.

### Applications and Datasets

The development of large-scale, diverse datasets has been crucial for benchmarking multimodal models. The CMU-MOSEI dataset introduced by Zadeh et al. (2018) has become a standard resource for multimodal sentiment analysis. In the medical domain, Johnson et al. (2023) released MIMIC-IV, a large electronic health record dataset that has spurred research on multimodal clinical prediction. Zhi et al. (2024) demonstrated the utility of multimodal approaches for predicting clinical outcomes from irregular electronic health record data, even in the presence of missing modalities.

### Summary

Collectively, these works highlight the progress and persistent challenges in multimodal learning with missing modalities and data scarcity. Our work builds on these foundations by proposing an in-context learning approach that dynamically borrows "treasures"—i.e., relevant knowledge—from neighboring examples or modalities, addressing both missing modalities and limited data conditions in a unified framework.
